content: Glucagon is a hormone naturally produced by the pancreas. It is prescribed to treat severe hypoglycemia (very low blood sugar levels). Additionally, it is used in certain diagnostic tests involving the stomach and other digestive organs. In some cases, glucagon may be prescribed for other purposes; consult your doctor or pharmacist for further details. Glucagon is typically administered via injection under the skin, into a muscle, or directly into a vein. It is supplied as a powder and a liquid, which must be mixed immediately before use. Detailed instructions for mixing and administering the injection are included in the medication package. Glucagon should be injected as soon as possible after identifying that a patient has lost consciousness due to low blood sugar. After administering the injection, the patient should be placed on their side to reduce the risk of choking in case of vomiting. Following the administration of glucagon, it is essential to contact a healthcare provider promptly. It is crucial for every patient to have a household member who is familiar with the symptoms of hypoglycemia and knows how to administer glucagon. If you frequently experience low blood sugar, it is recommended to carry a glucagon kit with you at all times. You should also be able to recognize the symptoms of hypoglycemia, which may include shakiness, dizziness, lightheadedness, sweating, confusion, irritability, sudden mood changes, headache, numbness or tingling around the mouth, weakness, pale skin, sudden hunger, or clumsy and jerky movements. If you notice these symptoms, try to consume a sugary food or drink, such as hard candy or fruit juice, before glucagon administration becomes necessary. Always follow the instructions on your prescription label carefully. If you or your household members have any questions, ask your doctor or pharmacist for clarification. Use glucagon exactly as prescribed, and do not use more or less of it or administer it more frequently than directed by your doctor. Before using glucagon, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to glucagon, any other medications, or products derived from beef or pork. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, including vitamins, that you are currently taking. Notify your doctor if you have a history of adrenal gland disorders, blood vessel diseases, malnutrition, pancreatic tumors, insulinoma, or pheochromocytoma. Additionally, let your doctor know if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Glucagon may cause side effects. Minor side effects include an upset stomach, vomiting, rash, or itching. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Severe side effects, such as difficulty breathing or loss of consciousness, require immediate medical attention. If you experience a serious side effect, you or your doctor can report it to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. Store glucagon in its original container, tightly sealed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat and moisture, and do not store it in the bathroom. Once the injection dose has been mixed, discard any unused portion. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Do not share your medication with others. If you have questions about refilling your prescription, consult your pharmacist. One brand name for glucagon is GlucaGen Diagnostic Kit®.
